title: Runbook: Mitigating KV Cache Fragmentation Incidents (Tail Latency / OOM / Alloc Failures)
author: Rafael Mendes
content:
## Purpose
This runbook covers triage and mitigation steps when KV cache fragmentation (or associated allocator/eviction churn) causes:
- p95/p99/p99.9 decode latency spikes (bursty, pool-local)
- Elevated request timeouts (Hosted API) or SLA breaches (Dedicated)
- GPU OOM events correlated with long-context or mixed-length traffic
- KV cache allocation failures, excessive evictions, or admission control flapping

The mitigations here are designed for safe operational response. This is not a substitute for performance debugging; for root cause and deep profiling, follow the profiling playbook linked above.

## Scope / systems
Applies to:
- Serving Runtime GPU pools (Hosted: multi-tenant; Dedicated: single-tenant pools)
- Scheduler admission control and backpressure
- KV cache allocator / prefix cache / eviction
- KV cache compaction feature (if enabled in the runtime build)

Not in scope:
- Full device-level defragmentation across restarts (we may restart workers as an emergency mitigation, but it is disruptive)
- Model correctness issues unrelated to allocator behavior

## Symptoms (common signatures)
### Customer-visible
- Bursty tail latency: median stable, but p99/p99.9 spikes during arrival bursts or context-length shifts
- Increased timeouts at the gateway with “upstream timeout” or “request deadline exceeded”
- Dedicated accounts report intermittent latency spikes with steady QPS

### Platform-visible
- KV cache fragmentation ratio rises steadily and does not recover after bursts
- Allocation failures spike (even with nominal free memory remaining)
- Eviction rate spikes (especially during decode-heavy periods)
- GPU memory high-water mark increases over time; OOM occurs when long-context traffic arrives
- Scheduler shows oscillating admission control (rapidly toggling accept/reject)

## Preconditions / access
- Observability: KV Cache Health dashboard (per region/pool/model family)
- Runtime config access (pool-scoped) via runtimectl / config service
- Ability to adjust routing weights (Hosted region/pool) and Dedicated pool settings
- Oncall paging: Runtime Oncall (Serving Runtime), Scheduler Oncall (if separate rotation)

## Quick triage checklist (10–15 minutes)
1) Confirm impact and scope
- Identify: Hosted vs Dedicated; affected region(s); specific pool(s); model family (e.g., llama-3.x, mistral)
- Validate it’s pool-local: compare p99 across pools in the same region
- Determine if it’s burst-driven (arrival spikes) or steady-state degradation

2) Open dashboards (minimum set)
- KV Cache Health dashboard:
  - Fragmentation ratio (per pool)
  - KV allocation failures (count / rate)
  - Eviction rate (blocks/sec or tokens/sec)
  - Compaction activity (if enabled): bytes moved, compaction time, budget utilization
  - Tail latency: p95/p99 decode latency per pool
- GPU memory / runtime metrics:
  - GPU memory used vs capacity
  - Worker restarts / OOM events
  - Scheduler admission control: reject rate, backpressure level

3) Classify the incident type
- Type A: Tail latency spike + high fragmentation + allocation failures (most urgent)
- Type B: Tail latency spike + high fragmentation, no alloc failures (mitigate before it turns into A)
- Type C: OOM events correlated with long-context traffic + fragmentation increasing
- Type D: Eviction thrash (eviction rate high, fragmentation high, throughput drops)

4) Capture key evidence for follow-up (do this early)
- Affected pool(s) + model + time window
- Screenshot or links to dashboard panels
- Current runtime flags relevant to KV cache (see “Safe flag changes”)
- Any concurrent changes: rollout, new model version, routing adjustments

## Immediate mitigation playbook (ordered by safety)
Start with the least risky, reversible changes.

### Step 1 — Reduce pressure on the affected pool (fast, safest)
Choose one or more:
- Shift traffic away from the hot pool
  - Hosted: reduce routing weight to the pool/region; shift to adjacent region if SLO allows
  - Dedicated: if customer has burst pool or overflow, route spillover there
- Scale out capacity (if available)
  - Add workers / GPUs to the pool to reduce per-worker cache pressure
- Tighten admission control temporarily
  - Prefer rejecting early rather than allowing allocator failure churn that poisons p99

Operational guidance:
- Make changes in small increments (e.g., 10–20% routing weight reduction), reassess after 5–10 minutes.
- Communicate to Support/CS for Dedicated: “temporary capacity management to stabilize tail latency.”

### Step 2 — Apply pool-level KV cache limit protections
Use when fragmentation is rising and/or memory high-water is approaching risk.

Actions (pool-scoped):
- Lower max active sequences / concurrency target for the pool
- Reduce maximum allowed context length (if policy allows; consider Dedicated contract constraints)
- Reduce speculative decoding settings (if enabled) that amplify KV usage
- Limit prefix cache footprint (if prefix caching is a contributor)

Notes:
- These actions may reduce throughput but stabilize latency and prevent OOM.
- For Dedicated: validate any changes against the customer’s negotiated limits; if uncertain, page Runtime Oncall before applying restrictive caps.

### Step 3 — Enable or tune KV cache compaction (only if runtime build supports it)
If the pool is running a build with compaction support and feature flag plumbing, enabling compaction can reduce fragmentation-driven allocation failures and tail spikes.

Pre-checks:
- Confirm compaction is available in the deployed runtime version for the pool.
- Check compaction dashboard panels exist for the pool (bytes moved, compaction time).
- Ensure you have rollback plan ready (Step 5).

Safe enablement pattern:
- Enable compaction in ONE pool (or shard) at a time.
- Start with conservative budgets (avoid median regression):
  - Prefer time/token budget enforcement over “run-to-completion” compaction.
  - Avoid aggressive triggers unless alloc failures are already occurring.

Recommended starting configuration (baseline):
- kv_cache.compaction.enabled = true
- kv_cache.compaction.trigger.fragmentation_ratio = 0.25
- kv_cache.compaction.trigger.on_alloc_failure = true
- kv_cache.compaction.budget.ms_per_sec = 2
- kv_cache.compaction.budget.max_bytes_per_interval = conservative (platform default)
- kv_cache.eviction.mode = "scheduler-aware-v1" (if available)

If alloc failures persist after 10–15 minutes:
- Increase compaction budget gradually (e.g., +1ms/sec steps)
- Lower fragmentation trigger threshold slightly (e.g., 0.25 → 0.20)
- Confirm compaction is actually running (budget not clamped, trigger firing)

If median latency regresses measurably after enablement:
- Reduce budget immediately or disable compaction (see rollback)

### Step 4 — Stabilize eviction behavior (reduce thrash)
Use when eviction rate is spiky and p99 is dominated by eviction/allocator churn.

Actions:
- Switch to scheduler-aware eviction (if not already) to avoid evicting “soon-to-be-used” sequences
- Increase eviction hysteresis / dampening (avoid rapid eviction oscillations)
- Reduce pressure from low-priority tenants (Hosted): temporarily deprioritize bursty low-tier traffic

Warning:
- Eviction changes can have fairness implications. Keep changes pool-scoped and reversible.

### Step 5 — Last resort: drain and restart workers (disruptive)
Use only when:
- Alloc failures are persistent and causing widespread timeouts
- OOM is repeated and auto-restart loops are occurring
- Compaction is unavailable or ineffective

Actions:
- Drain workers gradually to avoid capacity cliff
- Restart a subset of workers (start with 10–20%)
- Observe whether fragmentation and allocation failures reset

Risk:
- Restarting may trigger cold-start latency and reduce availability. Coordinate with Release Oncall if a rollout is in progress.

## Safe runtime flag changes (guardrails)
### General rules
- Prefer pool-scoped overrides; avoid global region-wide changes unless incident is region-wide.
- Change one dimension at a time; wait 5–10 minutes before stacking additional changes.
- Always note the “before” config values in the incident channel.

### Flags commonly used in KV cache fragmentation incidents
(Flag names may differ by runtime version; use runtimectl to list actual keys for the pool.)
- kv_cache.compaction.enabled (bool)
- kv_cache.compaction.trigger.fragmentation_ratio (float 0–1)
- kv_cache.compaction.trigger.on_alloc_failure (bool)
- kv_cache.compaction.budget.ms_per_sec (int/float)
- kv_cache.compaction.budget.max_bytes_per_interval (int)
- kv_cache.eviction.mode (enum: legacy | scheduler-aware-v1 | …)
- kv_cache.eviction.target_free_ratio (float)
- scheduler.cache_pressure.enabled (bool)
- scheduler.cache_pressure.reject_threshold (float)
- prefix_cache.max_bytes (int)
- runtime.max_active_sequences (int)

Example workflow (pseudo-commands)
1) Read current config
- runtimectl pool get-config --pool <POOL_ID> --keys "kv_cache.*" "scheduler.cache_pressure.*" "runtime.max_active_sequences" "prefix_cache.*"

2) Apply a pool-scoped override
- runtimectl pool set-config --pool <POOL_ID> --set kv_cache.compaction.enabled=true
- runtimectl pool set-config --pool <POOL_ID> --set kv_cache.compaction.budget.ms_per_sec=2

3) Verify rollout of config
- runtimectl pool config-status --pool <POOL_ID>
- Confirm workers have picked up new config (watch config revision metric/log)

## Rollback steps (must be ready before risky changes)
Trigger rollback if ANY of the following occur after a mitigation change (especially compaction enablement):
- p99 decode latency worsens by >15% for 10+ minutes vs pre-change baseline
- Median latency regressions exceed the SLO guardrail defined in SRE SLO page
- Allocation failures increase, or OOM frequency increases
- Error rate increases (timeouts, 5xx) beyond normal burst envelope

Rollback procedure
1) Revert the last change only (single-step back)
- runtimectl pool set-config --pool <POOL_ID> --set kv_cache.compaction.enabled=false
  or
- runtimectl pool set-config --pool <POOL_ID> --set kv_cache.compaction.budget.ms_per_sec=<previous>

2) If symptoms persist, revert to known-stable config bundle
- Apply the pool’s “baseline” config preset (document in pool config repo / defaults)

3) If the pool remains unstable, reduce traffic and drain
- Lower routing weights / increase admission control
- Consider worker restarts if OOM/alloc failures continue

4) Document rollback
- Record timestamp, config diff, and observed outcomes in incident channel

## When to page Runtime Oncall (Serving Runtime)
Page Runtime Oncall immediately if:
- KV allocation failures >0 for 5 minutes in a production pool AND p99 latency is elevated
- Any GPU OOMs correlated with request traffic in 10-minute window (not a one-off host issue)
- You suspect a compaction-related regression (compaction enabled and p99 worsens)
- Worker crashloop suspected due to allocator/compaction race (repeat restarts with similar signatures)

Page Scheduler Oncall (or Runtime Oncall if combined) if:
- Admission control is oscillating (reject rate swings) and cannot be stabilized with routing/limits
- Evidence suggests starvation/fairness pathologies after eviction changes

Information to include in the page
- Region + pool(s) + model(s)
- Start time and current severity (S0/S1/S2)
- Links to dashboard panels (KV cache health + tail latency)
- Recent config changes (flags and values)
- Whether compaction is enabled and current budget/trigger settings

## Communication / coordination
- Hosted incidents: notify #eng-sre and #eng-runtime; include routing changes and expected customer impact
- Dedicated incidents: notify Customer Success (and Support if active ticket exists) with:
  - affected account/pool
  - current mitigation (routing/caps)
  - expected timeline and next update

## Post-incident actions (within 24–48 hours)
- File or update follow-up ticket(s) with:
  - fragmentation ratio graphs and alloc failure counts
  - pool/model mix details (context length distribution, burst pattern)
  - whether compaction helped; recommended default changes
- If a new alert threshold was missing or noisy:
  - update KV Cache Health dashboard alerts and SLO page thresholds
- If a mitigation required manual intervention:
  - propose automation (e.g., automatic cache pressure routing, safer default budgets)

## Appendix: Common “gotchas”
- High GPU memory does not always imply fragmentation; verify fragmentation ratio and alloc failures.
- Eviction rate increases can mask fragmentation symptoms temporarily while degrading throughput.
- Restarting workers can appear to “fix” the issue by resetting allocator state, but does not address workload-driven fragmentation; treat as a stopgap.
- For Dedicated, ensure routing changes do not violate isolation expectations; prefer pool-local mitigations and coordinate with CS.

## Appendix: Metrics definitions (operational)
- Fragmentation ratio: fraction of KV cache capacity unusable due to holes / partially filled blocks (see runtime architecture page for exact formula).
- Allocation failures: count of failed KV allocation attempts (may trigger fallback paths or request rejection).
- Compaction bytes moved: total bytes relocated during compaction windows.
- Compaction budget utilization: fraction of allowed compaction work consumed; sustained 100% suggests under-budgeting or constant pressure.
